title: The Beatles file lawsuit to stop Alpha Omega compilation | 1973
content:
A lawsuit was filed on 16 February 1973 with the aim of preventing sales of a new and unauthorised Beatles compilation, Alpha Omega.

The suit was filed on behalf of The Beatles by George Harrison, in conjunction with Apple Records and Capitol Records.

Alpha Omega, or ΑΩ, was a four-part 8-track and quadruple vinyl compilation containing 60 Beatles songs, plus a handful of solo recordings. Produced by Audio Tape, Inc., it was an attempt to exploit the Sound Recording Amendment of 1971. The collection sold for $13.95, a low price made possible due to the lack of royalties paid to the artists.

The Sound Recording Amendment extended federal copyright in the US to recordings made on or after 15 February 1972, and declared that recordings made prior to then would remain subject to state or common law copyright. Based in New Jersey, Audio Tape, Inc. was able to exploit lax copyright laws in the state.

The Beatles’ $15 million lawsuit was filed in New York’s State Supreme Court. It mentioned two companies, Audio Tape and Electro, as well as Wisconsin company Economic Consultants, all of whom were accused of selling bootleg versions of Beatles recordings. Also named as defendants were the ABC network and the owners of WPIX-TV in New York, who had been accused of promoting the release via commercials broadcast on their services.
